## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle components can approach the streaming ceiling on death-free workloads.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS layout offers three loops very different hot fractions: loop 1 touches 24/68 B (35% hot), loop 2 only 8/68 B (11% hot), and loop 3 28/68 B (41% hot) — the remainder is dead weight dragged through every cache line. With no intermediate storage, the death verdict stays in registers, which is efficient for the decide step but means loop 3's render scatter reads and writes back into the same AoS structure at stride 68 B. The working set spills L1d at N≈963 and L2 at N≈61680; given that even the hottest loop touches under half the struct, the effective streaming demand is far below the raw 68 B/p, so cache capacity is less strained than the byte count suggests — but the low hot fraction also means any bandwidth the algo does move is largely wasted.

## Cache saturation
At q=0.01 the ns/p curve is strikingly flat: 7.8 ns/p at N=380 (L1d), 8.5 at N=10000 (L2), 7.5 at N=150000 (DRAM), and 8.2 at N=10M — no visible knee at either the L1d spill (N≈963) or the L2 spill (N≈61680). This flatness signals the algo is compute/overhead-bound, not cache-bound: the cost is set by instruction count and branch traffic, not data movement. The dense grid resolves both transitions but they are invisible because the per-particle work is 3.3–3.6× the memory floor. At higher death rates the curve is even flatter — branch overhead dominates uniformly across regimes.

## Bandwidth
The memory floor is 2.274 ns/p; at q=0.01 the algo runs 7.5–8.2 ns/p (3.3–3.6× the floor), achieving 8.3–9.1 GB/s — only 28–30% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling. This is compute/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. As q rises, achieved bandwidth falls to 4.8–5.2 GB/s (16–17% of ceiling) at q=0.5, and the bottleneck shifts from backend stalls (31.8% at q=0.01) to branch flushes (35.7% at q=0.5). Against baseline the edge is thin: 1.073× at q=0.01/N=380, collapsing to ~1.0× at q≥0.1 and even 0.957× at q=0.25/N=41000. Against the winner this algo is 1.7–2.6× slower everywhere, worsening with q — the winner's optimized LP2 handles respawn without the branch penalty.

## Assembly
Loop 1 carries the only vectorization: `dup.4s`, `fmul.4s`, `fadd.4s`, `ext.16b`, `ld1.s`, `fmul.2s`, `fadd.2s` — but just 9 vector instructions across the entire 295-instruction step, with an indexed gather present. Loops 2 and 3 are entirely scalar. Loop 2 has 11 conditional branches with branchy respawn (`b.ge`, `b.eq`, `b.gt` to `spawn`). Loop 3 has 15 branches, 18 `csel` selects, and 16 byte-granular `ldrb`/`strb` scatter pairs. The partial vec in loop 1 explains the marginal edge over scalar at q=0.01; the scalar byte-scatter and branchy respawn in loops 2–3 cap achieved bandwidth at ~30% of ceiling and drive the branch-flush collapse at high q.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo beats naive by only 1.073× at q=0.01/N=380 and falls to ~1.0× at q≥0.1 (0.957× at q=0.25/N=41000), while never exceeding half the winner's speed (1.7–2.6× slower). The 9 vector instructions in loop 1 cannot compensate for the entirely scalar, branch-heavy loops 2 and 3: at q=0.5 branch_flush reaches 35.7% and achieved bandwidth drops to 4.84 GB/s (16% of ceiling). The AoS stride-68B layout with 11–41% hot bytes wastes most streamed bandwidth, and the `strb` byte-granular scatter in loop 3 prevents any streaming benefit regardless of death rate.
